screens.title: Gross vs. net
screens.text: You worked 20 hours at $15 an hour, so you earned $300. That's your gross pay. What actually lands in your account is your net pay: gross pay minus taxes and deductions.

screens.question: Which is your take-home pay?
screens.explanation: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions. It's the money you can actually spend.

screens.title: Where it goes
screens.text: Almost every paycheck pays Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), together called FICA. Some states also take income tax, but Texas has no state income tax.

screens.question: You earn $300. FICA takes 7.65%. About how much is left before any income tax?
screens.explanation: 7.65% of $300 is about $23, which leaves about $277.

screens.question: If a teen earns only a little in a year, they may get federal income tax that was withheld back as a refund.
screens.explanation: If you earn less than the standard deduction, you usually owe no federal income tax. Filing a return gets withheld money back.

screens.question: Match each pay stub term.
screens.explanation: Reading your pay stub tells you exactly where your money went.

screens.question: Your budget should be based on your [___] pay.
screens.explanation: Plan with the money you actually receive: your net pay.

screens.title: Needs vs. wants
screens.text: A need is something you must have to live, work, or go to school. A want makes life more fun but you'd be okay without it. Most money problems start when wants get treated like needs.

screens.question: Which one is a need?
screens.explanation: Gas gets you to your job, which pays for everything else. The others are wants.

screens.question: Sort each purchase.
screens.explanation: Needs, wants, and saving are the three buckets every budget uses.

screens.question: Something can be a need but still have a "want" version.
screens.explanation: You need shoes. You want the $200 pair. The gap between them is where you can save.

screens.title: The 24-hour rule
screens.text: Before buying a want, wait 24 hours. If you still want it tomorrow, and it fits your budget, go for it. Lots of urges disappear overnight.

screens.question: You see a hoodie you love for $65. What's the smartest first move?
options: Buy it before it sells out
Wait a day and check your budget
Put it on a credit card
screens.explanation: Waiting a day gives you time to decide if it's worth the money, without pressure.

screens.question: A [___] is something you could live without, even if you'd miss it.
screens.explanation: Wants are fine in a budget. They just come after needs.

screens.title: A simple budget
screens.text: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it. The 50/30/20 rule is an easy start: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings.

screens.question: Match each part of the 50/30/20 rule.
screens.explanation: Needs first, then fun, and always something saved.

screens.question: You take home $400 a month. How much goes to savings under 50/30/20?
Same $400. How much can you spend on wants?
screens.explanation: 30% of $400 is $120. That's your guilt-free fun money.

screens.title: Track it
screens.text: A budget only works if you know where your money actually goes. For one month, write down every purchase. Most people are surprised by small things like snacks, delivery, and subscriptions.

screens.question: Small daily purchases don't really affect a budget.
screens.explanation: A $6 drink five days a week is about $120 a month. Small things add up fast.

screens.question: Put the budgeting steps in order.
screens.explanation: Budgeting is a loop: plan, track, and adjust.

screens.title: Designed to make you spend
screens.text: Apps and stores are built to make buying feel easy and urgent. Countdown timers, "only 2 left," and one-tap checkout all push you to buy before you think.

screens.question: "Sale ends in 10:00!" is mainly meant to…
screens.explanation: Urgency is a pressure tactic. A real deal will still be a deal after you think about it.

screens.question: Match each trick to how it works.
screens.explanation: Knowing the trick takes away most of its power.

screens.title: Subscriptions add up
screens.text: Streaming, music, games, and apps often cost $5–$15 a month each. Four of them can quietly cost $500+ a year.

screens.question: You pay for 3 subscriptions at $12 a month each. How much is that per year?
Saving your card in an app makes it easier to overspend.
screens.explanation: One-tap checkout removes the pause where you'd normally think twice.

screens.question: Before you buy, ask: is this a [___] or am I just being rushed?
screens.explanation: Slow down. If it's a real deal, it'll still look good after you think.

screens.question: Your paycheck says $500 gross, $462 net. What can you spend?
screens.explanation: Net pay is what actually reaches your account.

screens.question: Texas takes state income tax out of paychecks.
screens.explanation: Texas has no state income tax. You still pay FICA and possibly federal income tax.

screens.question: Sort each purchase.
screens.explanation: Needs keep you going, wants are fun, and saving protects your future.

screens.question: You take home $600 a month. How much goes to needs under 50/30/20?
"Only 2 left in stock!" Best response?
screens.explanation: Scarcity messages are designed to rush you.

screens.question: A budget is a plan for your money [___] you spend it.
screens.explanation: Planning first is what makes it a budget, not a receipt.

screens.question: Order the budgeting loop.
screens.explanation: Plan, track, and adjust every month.

screens.title: Save first, spend second
screens.text: Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month, which is usually nothing. Paying yourself first means moving money into savings the moment you get paid, before you spend any.

screens.question: When should savings come out of your paycheck?
options: At the end of the month
screens.explanation: If you save first, spending adjusts to what's left, not the other way around.

screens.question: Setting up an automatic transfer to savings makes saving easier.
screens.explanation: Automation removes willpower from the equation. The money moves before you can spend it.

screens.title: Goals make it real
screens.text: Saving is easier with a specific goal: "$1,200 for a used-car down payment by June" beats "save more." Divide the goal by the time you have to get a weekly target.

screens.question: You want $600 for a trip in 20 weeks. How much should you save each week?
screens.explanation: $600 ÷ 20 weeks = $30 a week.

screens.question: A good savings goal has a clear amount and a [___].
screens.explanation: A clear amount and date turn a wish into a plan.

screens.title: Life happens
screens.text: A cracked phone screen, a flat tire, a surprise bill. An emergency fund is money set aside only for surprises, so you don't have to borrow or panic.

screens.question: Which is a real emergency-fund expense?
options: Car repair to get to work
screens.explanation: Emergencies are unexpected and necessary. Sales and releases are wants.

screens.title: How much?
screens.text: Adults aim for 3–6 months of expenses. As a teen, start with a smaller goal, like $300–$500, and build from there.

screens.question: Without an emergency fund, a surprise bill often ends up on a credit card.
screens.explanation: And credit card interest can make that bill much more expensive.

screens.question: Your expenses are $1,500 a month. A 3-month emergency fund would be…
Order these from first to last.
items: Refill it after you use it
Grow it to a few months of expenses
correct_order: Refill it after you use it
Grow it to a few months of expenses
screens.explanation: Start small, refill when used, and grow it over time.

screens.title: Two main accounts
screens.text: A checking account is for everyday spending with a debit card. A savings account is for money you're keeping, and it usually pays you interest.

screens.question: Match each account to its job.
screens.explanation: Keeping savings separate makes it harder to spend by accident.

screens.question: Money in an FDIC-insured bank is protected up to $250,000 if the bank fails.
screens.explanation: FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per account type.

screens.title: Compare before you open
screens.text: Interest rates are shown as APY. Some savings accounts pay much more than others, so compare. Also watch for monthly fees and overdraft fees. Most teens under 18 open a joint account with a parent.

screens.question: Which savings account is best, all else equal?
screens.explanation: A higher APY and no fees means your money grows instead of shrinking.

screens.question: Spending more than you have in checking can trigger an [___] fee.
screens.explanation: Overdraft fees can be $30+ each time. Turn on low-balance alerts.

screens.title: Interest on your interest
screens.text: With compound interest, you earn interest on your money and on the interest it already earned. Over time, growth speeds up like a snowball rolling downhill.

screens.question: $1,000 earns 10% a year, compounded. How much after 2 years?
screens.explanation: Year 1: $1,000 → $1,100. Year 2: $1,100 → $1,210. The extra $10 is interest on interest.

screens.title: The Rule of 72
screens.text: Want to know how fast money doubles? Divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.

screens.question: Using the Rule of 72, how many years to double at 6%?
Starting to save at 16 instead of 26 can make a huge difference by retirement.
screens.explanation: Ten extra years means more doublings. Time is the biggest ingredient in compounding.

screens.question: What makes compound growth bigger?
screens.explanation: Time, rate, and how much you add all matter, but time is the one teens have the most of.

screens.question: Compound interest means earning interest on your [___].
screens.explanation: That's the snowball: your earnings start earning.

screens.question: "Pay yourself first" means…
options: Save as soon as you're paid
screens.explanation: Savings come out first, before spending.

screens.question: Save $25 a week. How much after 16 weeks?
An emergency fund is a good way to pay for a sale you don't want to miss.
screens.explanation: Emergency funds are only for real, unexpected needs.

screens.question: Match each term.
screens.explanation: These three terms show up on every bank account.

screens.question: Rule of 72: at 9%, about how many years to double?
screens.explanation: 72 ÷ 9 = 8 years.

screens.question: Which is the biggest advantage teens have for compounding?
screens.explanation: Starting early gives your money more years to grow.

screens.question: Checking is for spending; [___] is for keeping.
screens.explanation: Separate accounts keep your goals safe from everyday spending.

screens.title: Borrowed, not free
screens.text: A credit card lets you borrow money from a bank to pay now. Every swipe is a small loan you have to pay back later.

screens.question: You buy $60 sneakers with a credit card. Who paid the store?
options: The bank, as a loan to you
screens.explanation: The bank pays the store, and you now owe the bank $60.

screens.question: Match each card to how it works.
screens.explanation: Only a credit card spends the bank's money.

screens.title: The grace period
screens.text: Pay your full statement balance by the due date and you usually pay no interest. Leave some unpaid and interest starts adding up.

screens.question: If you pay the full balance every month, you usually pay no interest.
screens.explanation: Paying in full during the grace period avoids interest.

screens.question: Your credit [___] is the most you're allowed to borrow on the card.
screens.explanation: A $500 limit means you can't owe more than $500.

screens.question: Put a credit card month in order.
screens.explanation: Spend, get billed, then pay on time.

lessons.title: Interest & the Minimum Payment Trap
lessons.celebration: Interest & the Minimum Payment Trap complete.

screens.title: What APR means
screens.text: APR is the yearly interest rate on what you owe. Credit cards often charge 20% or more, which is far higher than most loans.

screens.question: You owe $1,000 at 24% APR and pay nothing for a year. About how much interest is added?
screens.explanation: 24% of $1,000 is $240, and compounding makes it a bit more.

screens.question: What's the minimum payment?
options: A fee for using the card
screens.explanation: It's the least you can pay to avoid a late fee. It's not the whole debt.

screens.title: The trap
screens.text: Minimum payments are small on purpose. Pay only the minimum and most of it goes to interest, so the debt can take years to clear.

screens.question: Paying only the minimum is a fast way to get out of debt.
screens.explanation: It keeps the debt alive for years and costs much more in interest.

screens.question: You owe $800. Which plan costs you the least?
screens.explanation: The sooner you pay it off, the less interest you pay.

screens.question: Missing a payment can add a late [___] on top of interest.
screens.explanation: Late fees, often around $30, make debt grow faster.

screens.title: Your money report card
screens.text: A credit score is a number from 300 to 850 that shows lenders how reliably you repay. Higher is better.

screens.question: What can a credit score affect?
screens.explanation: It affects loan rates, apartment approvals, and even some insurance.

screens.title: What goes into it
screens.text: The biggest factor is paying on time, at about 35%. Next is how much you owe compared with your limits, at about 30%.

screens.question: Match each FICO factor to its weight.
screens.explanation: New credit and credit mix make up the last ~20%.

screens.question: Using a small part of your credit limit is better for your score.
screens.explanation: Using less than about 30% of your limit helps your score.

screens.question: Under 18? A parent can add you as an authorized [___] on their card.
screens.explanation: It can help you start building credit history early.

screens.question: Which habit builds credit best?
screens.explanation: On-time payments are the biggest part of your score.

lessons.title: Buy Now, Pay Later & Loans
lessons.celebration: Buy Now, Pay Later & Loans complete.

screens.title: Split it into four?
screens.text: Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) splits a purchase into payments, often four. It feels small, but it's still debt.

screens.question: $200 headphones split into 4 payments. How much is each?
screens.explanation: $200 ÷ 4 = $50, due every couple of weeks.

screens.question: Missing a BNPL payment can lead to late fees.
screens.explanation: Missed payments can cost fees and may hurt your credit.

screens.title: Bigger loans
screens.text: Loans for big things like a car or college are paid back over years with interest. Student loans are common, so borrow only what you need.

screens.question: Match each loan to its use.
screens.explanation: Each one is borrowed money repaid with interest.

screens.question: A $10,000 car loan costs $1,500 in total interest. How much do you repay in total?
screens.explanation: $10,000 borrowed plus $1,500 interest = $11,500.

screens.question: Order the smart steps before borrowing.
items: Ask if you really need it
correct_order: Ask if you really need it
screens.explanation: Need it, shop the rate, check the budget, then borrow.

screens.question: What does using a credit card do?
screens.explanation: Every credit card purchase is a loan you repay.

screens.question: A typical credit card APR is around 2%.
screens.explanation: Credit card APRs are often 20% or higher.

screens.question: You owe $500 at 20% APR for a year. About how much interest is that?
screens.explanation: 20% of $500 is about $100.

screens.question: Credit scores range from 300 to [___].
screens.explanation: FICO scores run from 300 to 850.

screens.question: Biggest factor in your credit score?
screens.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score.

screens.question: BNPL payments are still a form of debt.
screens.explanation: You're borrowing now and repaying later.

screens.question: Match the term.
screens.explanation: Knowing these helps you avoid debt traps.

screens.title: A tiny piece of a company
screens.text: A stock (or share) is a small piece of ownership in a company. If the company grows, your piece can be worth more.

screens.question: Buying one share of a company means you…
options: Own a small part of it
screens.explanation: Shareholders are part-owners of the company.

screens.title: How stocks can pay you
screens.text: You can earn if the price rises and you sell, or from dividends, which are cash some companies pay to owners. Prices can also fall.

screens.question: A stock's price can go down as well as up.
screens.explanation: Stocks can lose value, and nothing is guaranteed.

screens.question: Match each term.
pairs: A loan to a company or government
screens.explanation: Stocks are ownership, and bonds are loans.

screens.question: Stocks are bought and sold on a stock [___].
screens.explanation: Examples are the NYSE and Nasdaq.

screens.question: Why might a stock's price rise?
screens.explanation: Prices move with what investors expect about future profits.

screens.title: Don't bet on one
screens.text: Diversification means spreading money across many investments. If one drops, the others can soften the hit.

screens.question: Which is more diversified?
screens.explanation: Owning many companies spreads out the risk.

screens.title: Index funds
screens.text: An index fund buys every company in a market index, like the S&P 500. One purchase gives you a slice of hundreds of companies.

screens.question: An S&P 500 index fund holds about 500 large US companies.
screens.explanation: It tracks the S&P 500, which has about 500 big US companies.

screens.question: The yearly fee a fund charges is called its expense [___].
screens.explanation: Lower expense ratios mean more of your money stays invested.

screens.question: Two similar index funds: 0.05% fee vs 1% fee. Which is better?
screens.explanation: Over many years, small fee differences add up to a lot.

screens.question: Match each to its risk level.
screens.explanation: More spread out usually means less risk from one company.

screens.title: Risk and reward
screens.text: Investments that can earn more usually come with more risk. Stocks swing more than savings accounts but have historically grown more over long periods.

screens.question: Historically, the US stock market has averaged about…
screens.explanation: Historically about 10% a year on average, but it's not guaranteed and some years drop.

screens.title: Time is your superpower
screens.text: Growth compounds: your earnings start earning too. At about 10% a year, money roughly doubles every 7 years.

screens.question: You invest $1,000 and it grows about 10% a year. Roughly how much after 7 years?
screens.explanation: At 10% a year it about doubles in 7 years, to roughly $1,950.

screens.question: Money you need next month is a good fit for stocks.
screens.explanation: Stocks can drop short term. Use them for goals years away.

screens.question: Order from lowest to highest risk.
screens.explanation: Higher potential return usually comes with higher risk.

screens.question: The market drops 15% this year. A long-term investor should usually…
options: Stay calm and stick to the plan
screens.explanation: Drops happen. Selling in a panic locks in losses.

screens.title: Can teens invest?
screens.text: Under 18 you usually can't open your own brokerage account. A parent can open a custodial account that they manage for you until you're an adult.

screens.question: A parent manages a [___] account for a minor.
screens.explanation: Custodial accounts hold investments for someone under 18.

screens.title: The Roth IRA
screens.text: A Roth IRA is a retirement account. If you have earned income, like from a job, you can put money in, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.

screens.question: You need earned income, like a paycheck, to put money in a Roth IRA.
screens.explanation: Contributions can't be more than what you earned from work that year.

screens.question: You earned $2,000 at a summer job. What's the most you can put in a Roth IRA this year?
screens.explanation: You can contribute up to what you earned, up to the yearly limit.

screens.question: Match the account.
screens.explanation: Different accounts fit different goals.

screens.question: Why start investing as a teen?
screens.explanation: Starting early gives compounding decades to work.

screens.question: Owning a stock means you own…
screens.explanation: Stocks are ownership. Bonds are loans.

screens.question: Diversifying means putting all your money in one stock.
screens.explanation: Diversifying means spreading money across many investments.

screens.question: An S&P 500 [___] fund holds hundreds of big US companies.
screens.explanation: Index funds offer instant diversification.

screens.question: At about 10% a year, roughly how many years does money take to double?
screens.explanation: Rule of 72: 72 ÷ 10 ≈ 7 years.

screens.question: Which fee is best for the same fund?
screens.explanation: Lower expense ratios leave more money growing.

screens.question: Stock returns of about 10% a year are guaranteed.
screens.explanation: That's a long-run historical average, not a promise.

screens.question: Match each to its use.
screens.explanation: You've got the investing basics down.

screens.title: What Is Crypto?
screens.text: Cryptocurrency is digital money tracked on a blockchain, a shared record copied across thousands of computers. No bank runs it, so no bank can reverse a mistake.

screens.question: What is a blockchain?
options: A shared record of transactions kept on many computers
An app that guarantees crypto prices
screens.explanation: A blockchain is a public ledger copied across many computers, not a bank.

screens.title: Big Swings
screens.text: Crypto prices can move fast. Bitcoin has historically dropped more than 50% several times. And unlike a bank account, crypto isn't FDIC-insured.

screens.question: You put $1,000 into a coin. It drops 50%, then rises 50%. How much do you have now?
screens.explanation: Down 50% leaves $500. Up 50% of $500 is only +$250, so you end at $750. Losses are harder to climb back from.

screens.question: If a crypto exchange goes bankrupt, the FDIC pays back your coins.
screens.explanation: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not crypto. When exchanges have collapsed, customers have lost money.

screens.question: When a meme coin's creators hype it up, then sell everything and vanish, it's called a [___].
screens.explanation: In a rug pull, insiders cash out and the price crashes, leaving everyone else holding coins worth almost nothing.

screens.question: Match each term.
screens.explanation: Knowing the words helps you see what you're actually buying.

lessons.title: Sports Betting & the House Edge
lessons.celebration: Sports Betting & the House Edge complete.

screens.title: The House Always Has an Edge
screens.text: Betting apps build a small cut, called the vig or juice, into every bet. It's small on one bet, but over many bets it adds up, which is how the house makes money.

screens.title: How -110 Works
screens.text: At -110 odds you risk $110 to win $100. Even if a game is a true coin flip, winning half your bets still loses money.

screens.question: At -110 odds, about what percent of bets must you win just to break even?
screens.explanation: 110 ÷ (110 + 100) ≈ 52.4%. Picking winners half the time isn't enough. You lose slowly.

screens.question: A game has a 5% house edge. You bet $10 a hundred times. About how much do you expect to lose?
screens.explanation: 5% of $10 is $0.50 per bet. Over 100 bets that's about $50 on average. This is called expected value.

screens.question: A betting app offers a "$200 free bet" to sign up. What's its main goal?
screens.explanation: Promos are marketing. They often have strings attached and are meant to turn you into a regular bettor.

screens.question: In most U.S. states that allow sports betting, you must be 21 to bet legally.
screens.explanation: Most legal states set the age at 21, a few use 18. Texas currently doesn't allow sports betting at all.

screens.question: Match each idea.
pairs: Paying for a random game reward
screens.explanation: Loot boxes use the same random-reward pull as gambling, even inside games.

screens.title: Why Hype Works
screens.text: FOMO, fear of missing out, makes people buy because everyone else seems to be getting rich. By the time a stock or coin is all over TikTok, the early buyers may be getting ready to sell.

screens.question: Your group chat says a stock is "going to the moon" and you need to buy today. What's the best first step?
options: Research what the company actually does and earns
screens.explanation: Hype isn't a reason to buy. Find out what you'd own, and never rush because of a deadline someone else made up.

screens.question: Put a pump-and-dump in order.
items: Insiders quietly buy a cheap stock or coin
They hype it online to pump the price
New buyers rush in with FOMO

Insiders sell and the price crashes
screens.explanation: The people hyping it profit from your buying. The late buyers are left with the losses.

screens.title: Finfluencers
screens.text: A finfluencer gives money advice on social media. Some are helpful, but some are paid to promote a product, and many never show their losses.

screens.question: If a finfluencer has millions of followers, their stock picks are probably reliable.
screens.explanation: Followers measure popularity, not accuracy. Check who's paying them and whether they show their losses too.

screens.question: Influencers who get paid to promote an investment are supposed to [___] it.
screens.explanation: Paid promotions should be disclosed, like #ad. If someone hides that they're paid, trust them less.

screens.question: Which is the strongest red flag in a money video?
options: They cite where their numbers come from
screens.explanation: Every investment has risk. Anyone promising no losses is selling something.

screens.title: Scams Target Teens Too
screens.text: Scammers use DMs, fake giveaways and "investment" offers. The warning signs are almost always the same: guaranteed profits, pressure to act fast, and requests for codes or passwords.

screens.question: A stranger DMs: "Send $50 in crypto, I'll trade it and send back $500 by Friday. Guaranteed!" What is this?
screens.explanation: Guaranteed 10x returns don't exist. Once you send crypto, you usually can't get it back.

screens.question: It's okay to share a 2FA code with someone claiming to be from your bank's support team.
screens.explanation: Real companies never ask for your password or 2FA code. Anyone who does is trying to get into your account.

screens.question: Match the scam to its trick.
pairs: Pay a fee to claim a prize
Fake login page steals your password
screens.explanation: Different stories, same goal: getting your money or your login.

screens.question: If an offer sounds too good to be true, it [___] is.
screens.explanation: Huge, fast, risk-free money is the classic sign of a scam.

screens.question: You think you got scammed. What do you do, in order?
items: Change your passwords and turn on 2FA
Tell a parent or trusted adult
correct_order: Change your passwords and turn on 2FA
Tell a parent or trusted adult
screens.explanation: Stop the damage, lock down your accounts, get help, then report it so others are warned.

screens.question: Which is true about crypto?
options: Its price is guaranteed by the government
Its price can swing 50% or more
screens.explanation: Crypto is volatile and not FDIC-insured. Bitcoin has historically fallen over 50% several times.

screens.question: You bet $20 a hundred times on a game with a 5% house edge. About how much do you expect to lose?
screens.explanation: 5% of $20 is $1 per bet, so about $100 over 100 bets. The house edge always wins over time.

screens.question: Winning exactly half your bets at -110 odds means you break even.
screens.explanation: At -110 you need about 52.4% wins to break even. At 50% you slowly lose to the vig.

screens.question: Buying something just because everyone online is hyping it is driven by [___].
screens.explanation: Fear of missing out pushes people to buy late, often near the top.

screens.question: Match each red flag.
pairs: Hype to sell to late buyers
screens.explanation: Each trick depends on you acting before you think.

screens.question: A finfluencer pushes a new coin but doesn't say they were paid. What should you assume?
options: They might have a hidden reason to promote it
Paid promotions are illegal, so it's fine
screens.explanation: Undisclosed promotion is a big warning sign. Their profit can come from your buying.

screens.question: Loot boxes use the same random-reward pull as gambling.
screens.explanation: Paying for a random chance at a prize is the core mechanic of gambling, even inside a game.

questionPool.question: Which is your take-home pay?
questionPool.explanation: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions. It's the money you can actually spend.

questionPool.question: You earn $300. FICA takes 7.65%. About how much is left before any income tax?
questionPool.explanation: 7.65% of $300 is about $23, which leaves about $277.

questionPool.question: If a teen earns only a little in a year, they may get federal income tax that was withheld back as a refund.
questionPool.explanation: If you earn less than the standard deduction, you usually owe no federal income tax. Filing a return gets withheld money back.

questionPool.question: Match each pay stub term.
questionPool.explanation: Reading your pay stub tells you exactly where your money went.

questionPool.question: Your budget should be based on your [___] pay.
questionPool.explanation: Plan with the money you actually receive: your net pay.

questionPool.question: Which one is a need?
questionPool.explanation: Gas gets you to your job, which pays for everything else. The others are wants.

questionPool.question: Sort each purchase.
questionPool.explanation: Needs, wants, and saving are the three buckets every budget uses.

questionPool.question: Something can be a need but still have a "want" version.
questionPool.explanation: You need shoes. You want the $200 pair. The gap between them is where you can save.

questionPool.question: You see a hoodie you love for $65. What's the smartest first move?
options: Buy it before it sells out
Wait a day and check your budget
Put it on a credit card
questionPool.explanation: Waiting a day gives you time to decide if it's worth the money, without pressure.

questionPool.question: A [___] is something you could live without, even if you'd miss it.
questionPool.explanation: Wants are fine in a budget. They just come after needs.

questionPool.question: Match each part of the 50/30/20 rule.
questionPool.explanation: Needs first, then fun, and always something saved.

questionPool.question: You take home $400 a month. How much goes to savings under 50/30/20?
Same $400. How much can you spend on wants?
questionPool.explanation: 30% of $400 is $120. That's your guilt-free fun money.

questionPool.question: Small daily purchases don't really affect a budget.
questionPool.explanation: A $6 drink five days a week is about $120 a month. Small things add up fast.

questionPool.question: Put the budgeting steps in order.
questionPool.explanation: Budgeting is a loop: plan, track, and adjust.

questionPool.question: "Sale ends in 10:00!" is mainly meant to…
questionPool.explanation: Urgency is a pressure tactic. A real deal will still be a deal after you think about it.

questionPool.question: Match each trick to how it works.
questionPool.explanation: Knowing the trick takes away most of its power.

questionPool.question: You pay for 3 subscriptions at $12 a month each. How much is that per year?
Saving your card in an app makes it easier to overspend.
questionPool.explanation: One-tap checkout removes the pause where you'd normally think twice.

questionPool.question: Before you buy, ask: is this a [___] or am I just being rushed?
questionPool.explanation: Slow down. If it's a real deal, it'll still look good after you think.

questionPool.question: When should savings come out of your paycheck?
options: At the end of the month
questionPool.explanation: If you save first, spending adjusts to what's left, not the other way around.

questionPool.question: Setting up an automatic transfer to savings makes saving easier.
questionPool.explanation: Automation removes willpower from the equation. The money moves before you can spend it.

questionPool.question: You want $600 for a trip in 20 weeks. How much should you save each week?
questionPool.explanation: $600 ÷ 20 weeks = $30 a week.

questionPool.question: A good savings goal has a clear amount and a [___].
questionPool.explanation: A clear amount and date turn a wish into a plan.

questionPool.question: Which is a real emergency-fund expense?
options: Car repair to get to work
questionPool.explanation: Emergencies are unexpected and necessary. Sales and releases are wants.

questionPool.question: Without an emergency fund, a surprise bill often ends up on a credit card.
questionPool.explanation: And credit card interest can make that bill much more expensive.

questionPool.question: Your expenses are $1,500 a month. A 3-month emergency fund would be…
Order these from first to last.
items: Refill it after you use it
Grow it to a few months of expenses
correct_order: Refill it after you use it
Grow it to a few months of expenses
questionPool.explanation: Start small, refill when used, and grow it over time.

questionPool.question: Match each account to its job.
questionPool.explanation: Keeping savings separate makes it harder to spend by accident.

questionPool.question: Money in an FDIC-insured bank is protected up to $250,000 if the bank fails.
questionPool.explanation: FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per account type.

questionPool.question: Which savings account is best, all else equal?
questionPool.explanation: A higher APY and no fees means your money grows instead of shrinking.

questionPool.question: Spending more than you have in checking can trigger an [___] fee.
questionPool.explanation: Overdraft fees can be $30+ each time. Turn on low-balance alerts.

questionPool.question: $1,000 earns 10% a year, compounded. How much after 2 years?
questionPool.explanation: Year 1: $1,000 → $1,100. Year 2: $1,100 → $1,210. The extra $10 is interest on interest.

questionPool.question: Using the Rule of 72, how many years to double at 6%?
Starting to save at 16 instead of 26 can make a huge difference by retirement.
questionPool.explanation: Ten extra years means more doublings. Time is the biggest ingredient in compounding.

questionPool.question: What makes compound growth bigger?
questionPool.explanation: Time, rate, and how much you add all matter, but time is the one teens have the most of.

questionPool.question: Compound interest means earning interest on your [___].
questionPool.explanation: That's the snowball: your earnings start earning.

questionPool.question: You buy $60 sneakers with a credit card. Who paid the store?
options: The bank, as a loan to you
questionPool.explanation: The bank pays the store, and you now owe the bank $60.

questionPool.question: Match each card to how it works.
questionPool.explanation: Only a credit card spends the bank's money.

questionPool.question: If you pay the full balance every month, you usually pay no interest.
questionPool.explanation: Paying in full during the grace period avoids interest.

questionPool.question: Your credit [___] is the most you're allowed to borrow on the card.
questionPool.explanation: A $500 limit means you can't owe more than $500.

questionPool.question: Put a credit card month in order.
questionPool.explanation: Spend, get billed, then pay on time.

questionPool.question: You owe $1,000 at 24% APR and pay nothing for a year. About how much interest is added?
questionPool.explanation: 24% of $1,000 is $240, and compounding makes it a bit more.

questionPool.question: What's the minimum payment?
options: A fee for using the card
questionPool.explanation: It's the least you can pay to avoid a late fee. It's not the whole debt.

questionPool.question: Paying only the minimum is a fast way to get out of debt.
questionPool.explanation: It keeps the debt alive for years and costs much more in interest.

questionPool.question: You owe $800. Which plan costs you the least?
questionPool.explanation: The sooner you pay it off, the less interest you pay.

questionPool.question: Missing a payment can add a late [___] on top of interest.
questionPool.explanation: Late fees, often around $30, make debt grow faster.

questionPool.question: What can a credit score affect?
questionPool.explanation: It affects loan rates, apartment approvals, and even some insurance.

questionPool.question: Match each FICO factor to its weight.
questionPool.explanation: New credit and credit mix make up the last ~20%.

questionPool.question: Using a small part of your credit limit is better for your score.
questionPool.explanation: Using less than about 30% of your limit helps your score.

questionPool.question: Under 18? A parent can add you as an authorized [___] on their card.
questionPool.explanation: It can help you start building credit history early.

questionPool.question: Which habit builds credit best?
questionPool.explanation: On-time payments are the biggest part of your score.

questionPool.question: $200 headphones split into 4 payments. How much is each?
questionPool.explanation: $200 ÷ 4 = $50, due every couple of weeks.

questionPool.question: Missing a BNPL payment can lead to late fees.
questionPool.explanation: Missed payments can cost fees and may hurt your credit.

questionPool.question: Match each loan to its use.
questionPool.explanation: Each one is borrowed money repaid with interest.

questionPool.question: A $10,000 car loan costs $1,500 in total interest. How much do you repay in total?
questionPool.explanation: $10,000 borrowed plus $1,500 interest = $11,500.

questionPool.question: Order the smart steps before borrowing.
items: Ask if you really need it
correct_order: Ask if you really need it
questionPool.explanation: Need it, shop the rate, check the budget, then borrow.

questionPool.question: Buying one share of a company means you…
options: Own a small part of it
questionPool.explanation: Shareholders are part-owners of the company.

questionPool.question: A stock's price can go down as well as up.
questionPool.explanation: Stocks can lose value, and nothing is guaranteed.

questionPool.question: Match each term.
pairs: A loan to a company or government
questionPool.explanation: Stocks are ownership, and bonds are loans.

questionPool.question: Stocks are bought and sold on a stock [___].
questionPool.explanation: Examples are the NYSE and Nasdaq.

questionPool.question: Why might a stock's price rise?
questionPool.explanation: Prices move with what investors expect about future profits.

questionPool.question: Which is more diversified?
questionPool.explanation: Owning many companies spreads out the risk.

questionPool.question: An S&P 500 index fund holds about 500 large US companies.
questionPool.explanation: It tracks the S&P 500, which has about 500 big US companies.

questionPool.question: The yearly fee a fund charges is called its expense [___].
questionPool.explanation: Lower expense ratios mean more of your money stays invested.

questionPool.question: Two similar index funds: 0.05% fee vs 1% fee. Which is better?
questionPool.explanation: Over many years, small fee differences add up to a lot.

questionPool.question: Match each to its risk level.
questionPool.explanation: More spread out usually means less risk from one company.

questionPool.question: Historically, the US stock market has averaged about…
questionPool.explanation: Historically about 10% a year on average, but it's not guaranteed and some years drop.

questionPool.question: You invest $1,000 and it grows about 10% a year. Roughly how much after 7 years?
questionPool.explanation: At 10% a year it about doubles in 7 years, to roughly $1,950.

questionPool.question: Money you need next month is a good fit for stocks.
questionPool.explanation: Stocks can drop short term. Use them for goals years away.

questionPool.question: Order from lowest to highest risk.
questionPool.explanation: Higher potential return usually comes with higher risk.

questionPool.question: The market drops 15% this year. A long-term investor should usually…
options: Stay calm and stick to the plan
questionPool.explanation: Drops happen. Selling in a panic locks in losses.

questionPool.question: A parent manages a [___] account for a minor.
questionPool.explanation: Custodial accounts hold investments for someone under 18.

questionPool.question: You need earned income, like a paycheck, to put money in a Roth IRA.
questionPool.explanation: Contributions can't be more than what you earned from work that year.

questionPool.question: You earned $2,000 at a summer job. What's the most you can put in a Roth IRA this year?
questionPool.explanation: You can contribute up to what you earned, up to the yearly limit.

questionPool.question: Match the account.
questionPool.explanation: Different accounts fit different goals.

questionPool.question: Why start investing as a teen?
questionPool.explanation: Starting early gives compounding decades to work.

questionPool.question: What is a blockchain?
options: A shared record of transactions kept on many computers
An app that guarantees crypto prices
questionPool.explanation: A blockchain is a public ledger copied across many computers, not a bank.

questionPool.question: You put $1,000 into a coin. It drops 50%, then rises 50%. How much do you have now?
questionPool.explanation: Down 50% leaves $500. Up 50% of $500 is only +$250, so you end at $750. Losses are harder to climb back from.

questionPool.question: If a crypto exchange goes bankrupt, the FDIC pays back your coins.
questionPool.explanation: FDIC insurance covers bank deposits, not crypto. When exchanges have collapsed, customers have lost money.

questionPool.question: When a meme coin's creators hype it up, then sell everything and vanish, it's called a [___].
questionPool.explanation: In a rug pull, insiders cash out and the price crashes, leaving everyone else holding coins worth almost nothing.

questionPool.question: Match each term.
questionPool.explanation: Knowing the words helps you see what you're actually buying.

questionPool.question: At -110 odds, about what percent of bets must you win just to break even?
questionPool.explanation: 110 ÷ (110 + 100) ≈ 52.4%. Picking winners half the time isn't enough. You lose slowly.

questionPool.question: A game has a 5% house edge. You bet $10 a hundred times. About how much do you expect to lose?
questionPool.explanation: 5% of $10 is $0.50 per bet. Over 100 bets that's about $50 on average. This is called expected value.

questionPool.question: A betting app offers a "$200 free bet" to sign up. What's its main goal?
questionPool.explanation: Promos are marketing. They often have strings attached and are meant to turn you into a regular bettor.

questionPool.question: In most U.S. states that allow sports betting, you must be 21 to bet legally.
questionPool.explanation: Most legal states set the age at 21, a few use 18. Texas currently doesn't allow sports betting at all.

questionPool.question: Match each idea.
pairs: Paying for a random game reward
questionPool.explanation: Loot boxes use the same random-reward pull as gambling, even inside games.

questionPool.question: Your group chat says a stock is "going to the moon" and you need to buy today. What's the best first step?
options: Research what the company actually does and earns
questionPool.explanation: Hype isn't a reason to buy. Find out what you'd own, and never rush because of a deadline someone else made up.

questionPool.question: Put a pump-and-dump in order.
items: Insiders quietly buy a cheap stock or coin
They hype it online to pump the price
New buyers rush in with FOMO
Insiders sell and the price crashes

They hype it online to pump the price
New buyers rush in with FOMO
Insiders sell and the price crashes
questionPool.explanation: The people hyping it profit from your buying. The late buyers are left with the losses.

questionPool.question: If a finfluencer has millions of followers, their stock picks are probably reliable.
questionPool.explanation: Followers measure popularity, not accuracy. Check who's paying them and whether they show their losses too.

questionPool.question: Influencers who get paid to promote an investment are supposed to [___] it.
questionPool.explanation: Paid promotions should be disclosed, like #ad. If someone hides that they're paid, trust them less.

questionPool.question: Which is the strongest red flag in a money video?
options: They cite where their numbers come from
questionPool.explanation: Every investment has risk. Anyone promising no losses is selling something.

questionPool.question: A stranger DMs: "Send $50 in crypto, I'll trade it and send back $500 by Friday. Guaranteed!" What is this?
questionPool.explanation: Guaranteed 10x returns don't exist. Once you send crypto, you usually can't get it back.

questionPool.question: It's okay to share a 2FA code with someone claiming to be from your bank's support team.
questionPool.explanation: Real companies never ask for your password or 2FA code. Anyone who does is trying to get into your account.

questionPool.question: Match the scam to its trick.
pairs: Pay a fee to claim a prize
Fake login page steals your password
questionPool.explanation: Different stories, same goal: getting your money or your login.

questionPool.question: If an offer sounds too good to be true, it [___] is.
questionPool.explanation: Huge, fast, risk-free money is the classic sign of a scam.

questionPool.question: You think you got scammed. What do you do, in order?
items: Change your passwords and turn on 2FA
Tell a parent or trusted adult
correct_order: Change your passwords and turn on 2FA
Tell a parent or trusted adult
questionPool.explanation: Stop the damage, lock down your accounts, get help, then report it so others are warned.

screens.question: Price reclaims the level, the retest holds, and buyer tape accelerates as offers thin. What's your decision?

WAIT would pass up a read where the evidence already aligns to act.
